name: Islamic philosophy as transmission rather than original speculation
plain_explanation: Russell argues that Arabic philosophy, for all its historical importance, was not original: its logic and metaphysics came from Aristotle and the Neoplatonists, its medicine from Galen, its mathematics and astronomy from Greek and Indian sources, and its mystical religious thought had an admixture of old Persian belief. Its great historical service was to preserve and transmit ancient learning through the 'dark ages' that separated ancient from modern European civilization.
precise_definition: Russell's thesis that Mohammedan (and, in a parallel way, Byzantine) civilization, while admirable in the arts and technical accomplishment, showed no real capacity for independent theoretical speculation, and functioned historically chiefly as a transmitter of ancient learning to the West, which then produced genuinely new thought (scholasticism from the Mohammedan stimulus, the Renaissance -- among other causes -- from the Byzantine one).
why_it_mattered: It frames how Russell wants readers to weigh Islamic philosophy's contribution: not for its own doctrines primarily, but for making the Aristotelian corpus and other ancient learning available to Western scholastics from the twelfth century onward.
historical_origin: Russell's own retrospective judgment, stated explicitly at the close of the chapter.
examples: Arabic writers showed real originality chiefly in mathematics and in chemistry (an incidental byproduct of alchemy)
Spanish Jews, who knew both Arabic and the Christians' language, served as translators bridging Moorish and Christian Spain
influence_on_later_thinkers: Set up the transmission of Aristotle (via Latin translations, e.g. of Averroes by Michael Scott in the early thirteenth century) that made possible the scholastic synthesis covered in the following chapters.
